prompt.context: Your client is Procter & Gamble, which owns Tampax and Always, leading menstrual product brands in the US. With the rise in sustainability-focused products, P&G's in-house R&D team has developed a hypoallergenic and eco-friendly high-grade silicone material for use in upcoming product launches. They are interested in using the material to make menstrual cups to add to their line of consumer care products.
prompt.question: Should P&G sell the silicone menstrual cups?

clarifying_info.q: What is the success criteria for launching this product?
clarifying_info.a: P&G will manufacture and sell the product if at least 10% of customers willing to purchase menstrual cups are willing to pay for it, and the inherent cannibalization does not negatively impact sales.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the current competitors in the menstrual cup space?
clarifying_info.a: Stand-alone brands such as Diva Cup, Softcup, Blossom, Saalt, and Lena.
Environmentally friendly with an average 5-year lifespan before recycling.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should I use?
clarifying_info.a: A compound discount rate for a 5-year period of 10%.
Assume even distribution from 0-80; menstruation starts at age 10 and ends at age 50.

clarifying_info.q: What is a comparable product price?
What is a reasonable market capture assumption?

framework: Pricing and Volume: market size for menstrual cups, consumer willingness to pay, competitor pricing, cannibalization of existing Tampax/Always sales
Marketing factors: sustainability positioning, price comparison vs. disposable products, long-term cost savings for consumers, target segments, portability and ease of use
Competition: standalone entrants (Diva Cup, Softcup, Blossom, Saalt, Lena), market saturation risk, P&G brand leverage
Risks: product cannibalization of core tampon/pad revenue, R&D cost recovery, manufacturing costs, lower-than-expected adoption

questions.prompt: Question 1: Calculate the US market size for menstrual cups.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a top-down approach: start with US population, filter to menstruating females by age, apply willingness-to-use rate, multiply by comparable price, then scale by market capture. Strong answer acknowledges assumptions and checks reasonableness.

math.setup: Top-down market sizing: US population -> female population -> menstruating age cohort -> willingness to use -> revenue at comparable price -> captured share
steps: Assume even distribution 0-80, so each 10-year band = 165M / 8 = 20.625M women per decade
Willingness to use (10%): 82.5M x 0.10 = 8.25M potential customers

questions.prompt: Question 2: Using Exhibit A (survey results), what adjustments would you make to your market size?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the survey shows 40% of respondents are undecided. P&G believes they can convert 25% of that undecided group, effectively adding 10% to willingness-to-use rate (from 10% to 20%). Strong answer adjusts market size upward and flags marketing importance for the undecided segment.

math.setup: Adjust willingness-to-use from 10% to 20% (original 10% + quarter of undecided 40% = 10% additional), recalculate market size
math.answer: Revised TAM ~$660M; Year 1 captured revenue: ~$66M (aggressive) or ~$33M (conservative). Use 16.5M addressable customers for subsequent calculations.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Part A): Using Exhibit B, calculate the annual cannibalized sales of P&G's existing menstrual care products per customer and in aggregate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual spend per customer across all three product types (tampons, pads, liners), then multiply by the captured customer base and then by the 5-year cup lifespan, applying the discount rate.

math.setup: Annual sales per customer = sum of (price x annual frequency) for each product. Aggregate by applying to captured market, then gross up for 5-year lifespan and discount.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Part B): Using Exhibit C, calculate estimated annual complementary product revenue and its 5-year present value.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual complementary product spend per customer (discs, wash, wipes), aggregate, gross up for 5 years, and discount.

math.setup: Annual complementary sales per customer = sum of (price x annual frequency). Aggregate and discount over 5-year lifespan.
steps: Total annual complementary spend per customer: $30 + $28 + $27 = $85/year

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Part C): Calculate the breakeven unit price for the menstrual cup to offset cannibalization.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up: Breakeven Price = (Cannibalized Revenue + R&D Costs - Complementary Revenue) / Captured Users. Strong answer notes this is the minimum price needed for launch to be financially neutral.

math.setup: Breakeven Unit Price = (Cannibalized Revenue PV + R&D Costs - Complementary Revenue PV) / Captured Customer Market

questions.prompt: Question 4: Using Exhibit D and the $30 breakeven price, evaluate whether P&G should launch the product.
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum respondents willing to pay $30 or more (Likely + Very Likely categories for $21-$30, $31-$40, $41-$50 ranges), plus 25% of Neither Likely nor Unlikely in those price bands, and compare to 10% of total respondents as the launch threshold.

math.setup: Count all respondents willing to pay >= breakeven price. Include 25% of undecided at relevant price points. Compare to 10% of total respondents (1,620).
steps: Neither Likely nor Unlikely at $21-$30: 260K; $31-$40: 156K; $41-$50: 104K -> NLU total: 520K
math.answer: 298K > 162K threshold; P&G should launch the product.

brainstorming.prompt: P&G has noticed consumers' increased interest in sustainability. What suggestions would you have for the marketing team to promote the menstrual cup? How can P&G lean into this consumer interest in their other menstrual products?

categories.name: Cup Marketing - Product
ideas: Emphasize ease of use and learning curve support (tutorials, guides)
Highlight hypoallergenic silicone material and safety credentials
Stress 5-year lifespan reducing waste vs. monthly disposables

categories.name: Cup Marketing - Pricing
ideas: Price according to customer WTP informed by survey data (~$30 breakeven)
Bundle with complementary products (wash, wipes) for trial promotion
Highlight long-term cost savings vs. lifetime spend on tampons/pads

categories.name: Cup Marketing - Place
ideas: Pharmacies and drugstores (existing Tampax/Always shelf relationships)
Subscription or starter kit bundles online

categories.name: Cup Marketing - Promotion
ideas: Influencer marketing targeting sustainability and wellness creators
Sustainability-focused ad campaign emphasizing zero monthly waste
Partner with environmental NGOs for credibility

categories.name: Non-Cup Products - Sustainability Push
ideas: Transition to fully biodegradable or compostable materials for pads/liners
Reduce and redesign packaging to minimize plastic
Transparency on product ingredients (no fragrances, organic cotton)
Develop organic product lines under Tampax/Always brands
Same quality messaging: 'the product you trust, now planet-friendly'
Sustainability-focused ad campaign for the broader menstrual care line

recommendation: P&G should launch the menstrual cup: 298K consumers willing to pay the $30 breakeven price exceeds the 10% threshold of 162K, and net cannibalization (after complementary product revenue offsets) is manageable at a ~$30 price point.
Recommended launch price: ~$30/cup, with potential to price higher as brand equity and sustainability positioning mature.
risks: Excessive product cannibalization of core Tampax and Always revenues if adoption exceeds projections
Incorrect revenue and purchasing frequency estimates in the model
Lower-than-expected market capture or slower consumer adoption of cups
New silicone material may have higher-value applications P&G has not yet explored
Switching cost for consumers unfamiliar with cup use may limit penetration
next_steps: Begin manufacturing and production planning for menstrual cups
Develop a comprehensive marketing plan emphasizing sustainability, cost savings, and ease of use; engage current retail partners for shelf placement
Develop complementary product line (wash, discs, wipes) to capture $85/year per cup customer
Consider expanding to international markets (especially developing markets; explore 1-for-1 donation model)
Monitor cannibalization rate quarterly and adjust pricing or bundling strategy if needed
